@context.rt.head: Heading of the "Route a storm" block under the storm drainage results.
@context.rt.dur: Field label: how many minutes the rain lasts.
@context.rt.auto: Placeholder of the duration box: the longest time of concentration is used.
@context.rt.idf: Placeholder of the intensity box: the rainfall curve at that duration is used.
@context.rt.none: Shown when there is nothing to route (no catchment drains to a structure).
@context.rt.storm: Line above the table; {d} minutes, {i} intensity, {u} unit.
@context.rt.r.in: Column: highest flow entering the pipe; {u} = flow unit.
@context.rt.r.out: Column: highest flow leaving the pipe; {u} = flow unit.
@context.rt.r.att: Column: how much lower the outgoing peak is than the incoming one.
@context.rt.r.ratio: Column: outgoing peak as a share of the pipe's full capacity.
@context.rt.r.when: Column: minutes from the start of the rain to the outgoing peak.
@context.rt.chart: Accessible name of the hydrograph chart; {q} {u} peak at {m} minutes.
@context.rt.csv: Button: download the outlet hydrograph as CSV.
@context.rt.method: Note under the results: what the routing does and does not do.
@context.rt.nodia: Problem: a pipe has no diameter, so it cannot be routed; {name}.
@context.rt.flat: Problem: a pipe has no fall or no length, so it cannot be routed; {name}.
@context.rt.long: Problem: the storm and the routing are longer than the longest run the tool simulates.
@context.rt.over: Problem: the routed peak is above the pipe's full capacity; {name}.
@context.ui.tb.measure: Toolbar button: measure distances and areas on the plan.
@context.meas.read.last: {bearing} = a survey bearing such as N 45°12'30" E.
@context.pl.prof.meas.read: Across = horizontal distance, up = height difference (negative = down), straight = the direct distance.
@context.pl.pack.region: Free text, for example France, Enedis, or a company name.
@context.pl.support.name: A support's short name on the plan: P1, P2… (P for pole). {n} = its number.
@context.pl.issue.at: {where} = the line, support, route or equipment (and the span), {what} = one of pl.issue.*.
@context.pl.rules.k: The formula stays as it is: k·√(sag + insulator) + kV/150.
@context.pl.don.untested: Keep "Untested" first. The other program is not named on purpose.
@context.pl.f.alpha_e6: Coefficient of linear expansion, in millionths per °C.
@context.pl.f.rts_n: The conductor's rated breaking strength (rated tensile strength).
@context.san.head: Heading in the pipe network's Properties when its type is Sanitary (0.6 LC.16).
@context.sw.head: Heading in the pipe network's Properties when its type is Sanitary (0.6 LC.16).
@context.san.maxfull: Setting label; a percent box follows.
@context.san.r.full: Table column: percent of full capacity.
@context.san.size.note: Note under the Size the pipes button.
@context.san.s.total: Structure Properties label: what flows out of it.
@context.san.p.pop: Pipe Properties label: people and area upstream.
@context.san.p.flat: Sanitary design problem (0.6 LC.16); {name} = a pipe.
@context.san.p.over: Sanitary design problem; percent of the pipe's full capacity.
@context.san.p.slow: Sanitary design problem; {v}, {min} are speeds (m/s or ft/s numbers).
@context.cv.qty.send.title: Tooltip of that button.
@context.cv.qty.cut: Item name written into the quantities file; TakeoffCraft shows it as the item's name.
@context.cv.qty.fill: Item name written into the quantities file.
@context.cv.qty.part: Note in the file, one per pad or corridor; {unit} = CY or m³.
@context.cv.len.bad: A number box refused what was typed; {text} = the typed text. 12'6" = 12 feet 6 inches.
@context.calc.err.char: Refusing a typed calculation such as 4+7/16 (0.6 DF.3). {text} = the character typed, {pos} = its place, 1 = first.
@context.calc.err.function: abs, round, ceil, floor are the function names to type: keep them as they are.
@context.why.overlap: Alignment design: PI = point of intersection; {a}/{b} = PI numbers; {need}, {ta}, {tb}, {dist} = lengths; {u} = the unit (ft or m).
@context.why.fix.r: Button that sets the curve radius at a PI to the largest that fits; R = radius.
@context.s3.label.point: A survey point's label in the 3D view: {n} = its number, {z} = its elevation.
@context.cad.units.scaled: A drawing's coordinates are multiplied into the project's units. {from} is a unit abbreviation such as mm or in.
@context.cad.closed: Layer name in the GIS layer list for the closed shapes of one CAD layer.
@context.cad.ui.what: {uses} is how many of the added layers have a use chosen.
@context.pp.north: North arrow letter on a sheet.
@context.touch.draft: Label of the button group over the plan on a touch screen while a line (alignment, pad, breakline…) is drawn: Finish = Enter, Undo point = Backspace, Cancel = Esc.
@context.scene.layer.cntr: Plan layer name (legend, layer lists): the alignment centerline.
@context.scene.layer.stan: Plan layer name: station ticks and labels along an alignment.
@context.scene.pad.label: Plan annotation at a pad (also in DXF/DWG/PDF); EL = elevation (drafting abbreviation). {name} = the pad name, {z} = its elevation.
@context.scene.pad.default: Default name of a pad with no name (plan annotation).
@context.scene.sta.pc: Plan annotation at the start of a curve: PC = point of curvature (drafting abbreviation); {sta} = station such as 12+34.56.
@context.scene.sta.pt: Plan annotation at the end of a curve: PT = point of tangency (drafting abbreviation); {sta} = station.
@context.scene.al.default: Default label of an alignment with no name (plan annotation at its start).
@context.scene.strc.rim: Plan annotation at a pipe structure; RIM = rim elevation (drafting abbreviation). {name} = structure name, {rim} = elevation.
@context.units.ft: Name of the project unit (US survey feet).
@context.thin.spacing: Error when thinning LiDAR or grid points: the cell spacing typed is not a positive number.
@context.dxf.renamed: Note after a DXF export: layer names that R12 DXF cannot hold were renamed. R12 is the DXF version.
@context.al.err.back: Alignment error; PI = point of intersection, {pi} = its number.
@context.al.err.overlap: Alignment error; {a} and {b} = PI numbers, {need} and {dist} = lengths in project units.
@context.prof.err.two: Profile error; PVI = point of vertical intersection; {sta} = the station.
@context.prof.err.before: Profile error; {pvi} = PVI number, {len} = the vertical curve length (L).
@context.prof.err.past: Profile error; {pvi} = PVI number, {len} = the vertical curve length (L).
@context.xml.err.mismatch.open: Error reading an XML (LandXML) file; {tag} = the closing tag found, {open} = the element still open.
@context.xml.err.tag: Error reading an XML file; {tag} = the element, such as <Point>.
@context.xml.err.cdata: Error reading an XML file: a CDATA section is not closed (CDATA is an XML term).
@context.xml.err.pi: Error reading an XML file: a <?…?> processing instruction is not closed (XML term).
@context.pv.ve: Profile view corner label; {ve} = the factor, such as 5.
@context.pv.lk: Profile view label at a vertical curve: L = curve length {len}, K = rate of curvature {k} (road design symbols).
@context.pv.high: Profile view label at the high point of a crest curve: {sta} = station, {z} = elevation.
@context.pv.low: Profile view label at the low point of a sag curve: {sta} = station, {z} = elevation.
@context.pv.pvi: Profile view label at a PVI (point of vertical intersection): {sta} = station, {z} = elevation.
@context.plot.paper.letter: Paper size in the PDF plot list.
@context.plot.title: Default title of a plotted PDF sheet when the project has no name.
@context.plot.scale: PDF sheet title strip; {scale} = the scale, such as 1" = 40' or 1:500.
@context.plot.made: PDF sheet title strip, bottom right; {date} = the plot date (YYYY-MM-DD).
@context.pipes.default: Default name of a new storm pipe network.
@context.pipes.p.cover.along: {cover} = depth of cover, {at} = distance from the upper end, {min} = the minimum cover (all in project units).
@context.pipes.s.drop.above: {name} = structure; {out}/{outInv} = the outgoing pipe and its invert; {in}/{inInv} = an incoming pipe and its invert.
@context.pipes.s.drop.less: {drop} = the minimum drop across a structure (project units); other fills as pipes.s.drop.above.
@context.pipes.noground: Setting inverts automatically: {name} = pipe, {at} = its upstream structure.
@context.grade.bl.edge: Name of the breakline along a graded pad's edge; {name} = the pad name.
@context.grade.bl.daylight: Name of the breakline along a graded pad's daylight line (where its slopes meet the ground); {name} = the pad name.
@context.gtw.too_many: GeoTIFF export refusal. {w} and {h} = grid columns and rows (formatted), {cells} = cells in millions (one decimal), {max} = the limit in millions.
@context.pts.bad.cols: Why a row of a point file was not read (lower case, shown after "Line 12: "); {n} = columns found, {want} = columns expected, {format} = the column order such as PNEZD.
@context.pts.bad.ne: Why a row of a point file was not read (lower case, after "Line 12: ").
@context.pts.bad.twice: Why a row of a point file was not read; {num} = the point number.
@context.clip.why.newer: Where pasted points came from (lower case): text copied after CivilCraft's own copy.
@context.clip.why.own: Where pasted points came from: points copied inside CivilCraft.
@context.clip.why.unread: {why} = the reason the first row was not read (lower case), or "no rows".
@context.clip.kept: Part of the paste message, joined with "; " to clip.changed; {n} = pasted points that kept their numbers.
@context.clip.changed: Part of the paste message; {n} = renumbered points, {was} and {now} = number ranges such as 1–2 and 11–12.
@context.terrain.unit.m: Unit word inside sentences about an elevation grid (lower case), e.g. "Elevations converted from meters".
@context.terrain.crs.unknown: {code} = the EPSG number the file names.
@context.raster.not_tiff: Error opening a GeoTIFF. {reason} = the reader library's own message (English, technical).
@context.raster.bad_cells: {bits} = bits per sample (8, 16, 32…), {fmt} = the TIFF SampleFormat code.
@context.raster.zfrom.band: Shown where the import dialog says where the elevation unit came from ("Elevations in feet, from …"). {unit} = the unit name as written in the file.
@context.raster.zfrom.key: Shown where the import dialog says where the elevation unit came from ("from …"). A GeoTIFF VerticalUnitsGeoKey.
@context.raster.too_big: {name} = the file name, {mb} = its size in MB, {max} = the limit in MB.
@context.raster.area_big: {cells} and {max} are counts already formatted, e.g. "12.5 million".
@context.raster.read_failed: {reason} = the reader library's own message (English, technical).
@context.raster.asc.short: {read} and {total} are value counts already formatted.
@context.raster.big.billion: A large count of cells written in words; {n} = the number with one decimal (e.g. "1.2 billion").
@context.raster.big.million: A large count of cells written in words; {n} = the number with one decimal (e.g. "12.5 million").
@context.tin.badfaces: Note after reading a surface from a file (LandXML faces = triangles).
@context.raster.bands_n: Note when a GeoTIFF elevation grid has several bands (n is 2 or more in practice).
@context.lx.err.root: {tag} = the XML root element found, such as <svg>.
@context.lx.unit.m: {unit} = the unit name the LandXML file gives.
@context.lx.def.surface: Name given to a surface read from LandXML that has none.
@context.lx.def.breakline: Name given to a breakline read from LandXML that has none.
@context.lx.def.profile: Name given to a profile read from LandXML that has none.
@context.lx.def.network: Name given to a pipe network read from LandXML that has none.
@context.lx.surf.type: {type} = the LandXML surface type (such as grid); TIN = triangulated irregular network.
@context.lx.net.type: {type} = the pipe network type the file names (LandXML value).
@context.lx.notyet: {what} = a LandXML element name such as Parcels or Roadways (kept in English).
@context.las.class.0: ASPRS LiDAR point class 0, listed in the point cloud import dialog's class table.
@context.las.class.12: ASPRS LiDAR point class 12 (points from overlapping flight lines), in the import dialog's class table.
@context.las.class.6: ASPRS LiDAR point class (a building), in the import dialog's class table.
@context.las.class.9: ASPRS LiDAR point class (water), in the import dialog's class table.
@context.las.class.10: ASPRS LiDAR point class (railway), in the import dialog's class table.
@context.las.bad.version: {version} = major.minor read from the file, e.g. 2.0.
@context.las.short: {available} and {count} are point counts already formatted.
@context.las.crs.bad_why: {reason} = the coordinate-system reader's own message, which ends with its own full stop.
@context.las.laz.stopped: {read} and {n} are point counts already formatted.
@context.gstate.bad.features: Note after opening a project file; {layer} = the GIS layer's name.
@context.layers.default: Name given to a GIS layer that has none.
@context.project.untitled: Default name of a new project (the Name field under Site).
@context.surface.eg: Name of the existing-ground surface (the surface built from the survey).
@context.project.corridor: Name of an alignment's corridor in the graded surface; {name} = the alignment name.
@context.project.def.structure: Name given to a pipe structure with none, read from a project file.
@context.project.def.pipe: Name given to a pipe with none, read from a project file.
@context.project.def.crs: Name given to a coordinate system with none, read from a project file.
@context.project.bad.points: Note when opening a project file; the English says "points" for 1 too (kept as it was).
@context.geom.type: {type} = the WKB geometry type number from the file.
@context.dbf.cpg.unknown: {cpg} = the text of the shapefile's .cpg file (an encoding name).
@context.dbf.cut: {n} = the record count the file states, {avail} = the records it actually holds.
@context.surface.fg: Name of the proposed surface: the existing ground with pads, corridors and feature lines graded in.
@context.s3.contours.minor: Name of a line set in the 3D view and in GLB/OBJ exports; {surface} = Existing ground or Graded surface.
@context.s3.alignments: Name of a line set in the 3D view and in GLB/OBJ exports.
@context.s3.roads: Name of the road surfaces (lanes, curbs, walks from a corridor) in the 3D view and in exports.
@context.sides.w.tall: Warning on a pad or platform: {name} = its name, {h} = the tallest wall, {limit} = the height set to warn above, {u} = ft or m.
@context.sides.wall.h: Plan label: a retaining wall's height {h} at that point (number only).
@context.sides.slope: A slope: {h} horizontal to 1 vertical, also as percent and degrees.
@context.s3.warning: 3D view note for a warning about one item: {name} = the item (e.g. Main street corridor), {text} = the warning.
@context.corr.standin: Warning on a corridor built with no survey: {z} = the elevation of the flat stand-in ground (the design profile's average), {unit} = ft or m.
@context.corr.standin.zero: As corr.standin, when the alignment has no design profile either: road and ground at elevation {z}.
@context.s3.plants: Name of the plants (Landscape workspace) in the 3D view and in exports.
@context.s3.plants.unknown: 3D view note: plants whose species is not in the plant list; {n} = how many.
@context.v3d.show.roads: 3D view Show menu item: the road body built by corridors.
@context.s3.point: What a click in the 3D view picked; {n} = the survey point number.
@context.shp.noshp: {name} = the shapefile's name without extension (as in every shp.* message).
@context.shp.note: Prefixes a note from reading the .dbf with the shapefile's name; {note} = that note.
@context.shp.cut: {rec} = the 1-based number of the shape (record) in the file.
@context.geojson.crs.member: {crs} = the coordinate system name written in the file. Keep "crs" as is (a GeoJSON member name).
@context.geojson.layer.pt: Layer name when one GeoJSON file holds several kinds of geometry; {name} = the file's name.
@context.zip.method: {file} = a file name inside the zip; {method} = the compression method number.
@context.v3d.view.iso: 3D view bar, Standard view list: the isometric view (short).
@context.v3d.view.top: 3D view bar, Standard view list: looking from the top.
@context.v3d.view.back: 3D view bar, Standard view list: looking from the back (north).
@context.v3d.view.left: 3D view bar, Standard view list: looking from the left (west).
@context.v3d.extents: 3D view bar button: zoom to show everything.
@context.v3d.exag.opt: Option in the 3D view's exaggeration list; {x} = 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10.
@context.v3d.show: 3D view bar menu button listing what to draw.
@context.v3d.export: Label before the GLB and OBJ buttons on the 3D view bar.
@context.v3d.tip.at: 3D view hover tip: E = easting, N = northing, EL = elevation; {u} = unit symbol (ft or m).
@context.v3d.exported: Status after a 3D export; {file} = file name, {e} {n} {z} = the origin's easting, northing, elevation.
@context.tui.crs.not_stated: Value in the import dialog's facts, after "Coordinate system": the file names no system.
@context.tui.keep.nearest: Option of the "Keep" select (LiDAR import): which point each cell keeps.
@context.tui.keep.nearest.in: Same choice as tui.keep.nearest, inside the result sentence tui.done.lidar (lower case, in brackets).
@context.tui.keep.lowest.in: Same choice as tui.keep.lowest, inside the result sentence tui.done.lidar (lower case, in brackets).
@context.tui.keep.average.in: Same choice as tui.keep.average, inside the result sentence tui.done.lidar (lower case, in brackets).
@context.tui.l.area: Label of the import dialog's area select (which part of the file to read).
@context.tui.l.thin: Label of the spacing input; {unit} = m or ft.
@context.tui.l.keep: Label of the LiDAR select choosing which point each cell keeps (verb).
@context.tui.ll.range: Extent in latitude/longitude; each fill is a formatted angle such as 40.12345° N.
@context.tui.f.kind: Label in the file facts (file type).
@context.tui.kind.las: {format} = LAS or LAZ, {version} = e.g. 1.4, {pf} = point format number.
@context.tui.cells: {w}, {h} = columns and rows; {total} = their product in words, e.g. 12.5 million.
@context.tui.f.nodata: Label in the file facts; the value is the file's no-data number.
@context.tui.f.cells_are: Label in the file facts; value tui.cells_are.points.
@context.tui.f.z: Label in the file facts; value "{min} to {max}".
@context.tui.crs.head: Heading of the import dialog's coordinate system section, and a label in its facts.
@context.tui.class.aria: Accessible name of a class checkbox; {c} = the class number.
@context.tui.class.reserved: LiDAR class with no standard name (19–63).
@context.tui.class.user: LiDAR class 64–255, defined by the data maker.
@context.tui.over.grid: Follows tui.plan.points in the same message; {cap} = the limit, {d} {unit} = a spacing.
@context.tui.plan.lidar: {count} = points kept, {sp} {unit} = spacing, {inside} = points in the area.
@context.tui.z.as: One part of tui.z.info: {word} = meters/feet (lower case), {min} {max} {unit} = project elevations.
@context.tui.z.says_from: {word} = the unit word; {from} = where it came from, e.g. "the file’s vertical unit key".
@context.tui.done.dem: Plural by {n} = the step (every n-th cell). {count} = points, {d} {unit} = spacing.
@context.tui.points.reading_pct: {pct} = percent read; {kept} = points kept so far.
@context.tui.done.zconv: {word} = the file's unit word; {f} = the factor.
@context.tui.gt.z: {word} = the project's elevation unit word (lower case).
@context.tui.gt.info: {total} = cells in words, e.g. 1.2 million; {mb} = size estimate.
@context.tui.cancelled: Progress line of the GeoTIFF export after Cancel.
@context.tui.l.surface: Label of the surface select in the GeoTIFF export.
@context.tui.gt.head: Heading of the GeoTIFF section inside the GIS › Export dialog.
@context.gpkg.load: {status} = the HTTP status number of the failed download.
@context.gpkg.max: {table} = the GeoPackage table's name (as in every gpkg.* message).
@context.gpkg.layer.pt: Layer name when one GeoPackage table holds several kinds of geometry.
@context.gpkg.geom.env: A GeoPackage geometry's bounding-box header is invalid.
@context.gpkg.geom.short: A GeoPackage geometry is cut short.
@context.tui.plan.pts: Live count in the grid import dialog; plural by {n} = the step (every n-th cell; English ordinal ending). {count} = points, {w} × {h} = cells, {d} {unit} = spacing.
@context.tui.plan.tin: As tui.plan.pts when the grid becomes the surface; {tri} = triangles.
@context.crs.load: {status} = the HTTP status number of the failed download.
@context.crs.prj.name: Name given to a coordinate system read from a .prj file that names none.
@context.set.order: Settings › CivilCraft: heading of the choice of column order for point rows (P = point, N = northing, E = easting, Z = elevation, D = description).
@context.set.renum.clash: Settings option: pasted points keep their numbers unless a point already has that number.
@context.set.start.ph: Placeholder of the "New numbers start at" box when empty: the next unused number is used.
@context.set.labels.n: Settings option: a point label shows only the point number.
@context.set.internet.off: Settings option: map layers from the internet are off.
@context.set.internet.on: Settings option: map layers from the internet are on.
@context.crs.unit.m: The unit of a coordinate system, in the coordinate system dialog.
@context.crs.area.none: A coordinate system's area of use when the catalog gives none.
@context.crs.area.box: Area of use of a coordinate system; each fill is an angle with its hemisphere letter, e.g. 30.25° N.
@context.crs.shift.same: {acc} = a distance with its unit, e.g. 2 m or 50 cm.
@context.crs.local.ground: {scale} = the combined scale factor; {e}, {n} = the base point's easting and northing; E/N = easting/northing.
@context.mapl.http.status: {status} = the HTTP status code, sometimes followed by the server's own status text (English).
@context.mapl.err.sent: {type} = a MIME type such as text/html.
@context.mapl.err.sent_why: {type} = a MIME type; {why} = the start of the server's own message.
@context.mapl.err.stopped: Follows a network error message in the same note, on the map layer's row.
@context.mapl.world.none: {a}, {b} = world file names to look for, e.g. plan.pgw and plan.pngw.
@context.mapl.where.text_nopc: “Project coordinates” must match the button mapl.where.project_coords.

@context.mapl.default_name: Name given to a map layer that has none; saved in the project.
@context.mapl.kind.xyz: Option of the "From" select; {z}/{x}/{y} are literal URL placeholders (written {{z}} here).
@context.mapl.from: Label of the select choosing the kind of map layer to add.
@context.mapl.layers: Heading of the list of map layers in the Map layers dialog.
@context.mapl.row.proj_coords: Shown after the layer kind on its row ("Picture · project coordinates"), lower case.
@context.mapl.opacity: Label before the opacity slider of a map layer.
@context.mapl.kind.tiles: Kind of map layer shown on its row (an XYZ tile server).
@context.mapl.kind.picture: Kind of map layer shown on its row (a picture from a file).
@context.mapl.help.xyz: {z} {x} {y} {-y} {s} are literal URL placeholders (written with double braces here).
@context.mapl.wms.found: {title} = the server's title, {version} = the WMS version, n = layers offered.
@context.mapl.arc.service: Default title of an ArcGIS service that names none.
@context.mapl.arc.tiled: {name} = the service name, {kind} = MapServer or ImageServer.
@context.mapl.f.layer: Label of the select of a server's layers.
@context.mapl.stop: Button that stops reading a map server.

@context.gread.src.wgs84: The coordinate system of an imported GIS source, shown in the layer's details.
@context.gread.src.bad: The coordinate system of an imported GIS source when it could not be read.

@context.gread.z: {from}, {to} = unit words (metres, feet, US survey feet).

@context.gread.lx.epsg: Fragment: fills {why} in “… names a coordinate system, but {why}; the project has none.”
@context.gread.lx.name: Fragment: fills {why} in “… names a coordinate system, but {why}; the project has none.”
@context.gread.lx.noname: Shown inside quotes when a LandXML coordinate system has no name.
@context.gread.undo: Undo step name; {file} = the imported file's name.

@context.ui.tb.gis-import: Button in the GIS toolbar group: import GIS data.

@context.cv.dwg.n.poly3d: DWG export count, filled into a list.

@context.lx.al.spitype: LandXML import note; {name} = alignment name, {type} = the file's spiral type (e.g. cubic, bloss).
@context.se.spiral.steep: Superelevation problem; {n} = curve number, {end} = TS or ST (drafting abbreviations: tangent-to-spiral, spiral-to-tangent), {ls} and {need} = lengths.
@context.scene.sta.ts: Plan annotation: TS = tangent to spiral (drafting abbreviation); {sta} = station.
@context.scene.sta.sc: Plan annotation: SC = spiral to curve; {sta} = station.
@context.scene.sta.cs: Plan annotation: CS = curve to spiral; {sta} = station.
@context.scene.sta.st: Plan annotation: ST = spiral to tangent; {sta} = station.
@context.cv.al.col.ls1: Column heading in the PI table: length of the spiral that leads into the curve.
@context.cv.al.col.ls2: Column heading in the PI table: length of the spiral that leads out of the curve.

@context.as.high: Unit text after a curb's height.
@context.as.up: Accessible name of the button that moves a part toward the centreline.
@context.as.add.type: Accessible name of the list of part types to add to one side.
@context.crs.pick.matched: {code} = EPSG number, {name} = the catalog system's name.
@context.crs.pick.same: {list} = EPSG numbers of systems with the same projection maths, comma-separated.
@context.geo.pick.hit: One result row: {code} = EPSG number, {name} = system name, {unit} = m, ft or ftUS.
@context.geo.pick.custom: {name} = the definition's name, {unit} = its linear unit (m, ft, ftUS).

fl.offset.zero: Type an offset distance other than 0.
fl.offset.repeat: The feature line has two vertices in the same place: remove one first.
fl.offset.sharp: A corner turns back too sharply to offset it.
fl.offset.fold: At that distance the offset folds over itself at a bend: use a smaller distance.
toolbar.feature.title: Draw a feature line: a 3D line you grade vertex by vertex, used as a breakline or graded into the design (L)
sw.head: Swept path
sw.f.name: Name
sw.mode.forward: Forward: the front axle follows the line
sw.mode.reverse: Reversing: the last axle follows the line
sw.mode.note: Draw the line in the direction of travel. Reversing, CivilCraft works out the steering the tractor needs and checks it against the lock.
sw.f.bad: Give every size a number: widths and wheelbases above 0, the lock under 89°.
sw.placeholders: The vehicles to start from are placeholders, not a standard: set the sizes from your own design vehicle.
sw.done: {name}: driven along the line within the steering lock and the articulation limits.
sw.done.problems: {name}: {n} problem(s) along the line; see Properties.
sw.noline: The line this swept path follows is gone or has errors.

sw.prob.steer: At {s} {u} the steering needs {v}°, past the lock of {max}°.
sw.prob.articulation: At {s} {u} trailer {n} turns {v}° against the unit ahead, past its limit of {max}° (it jackknifes).

fl.click.ground: Vertex {n}: its elevation comes from the ground. Enter finishes.
fl.need2: A feature line needs at least two vertices.
fl.need3: A closed feature line needs at least three vertices.
fl.name: Feature line {n}

fl.drawn.guessed.one: 1 vertex was off the surface and took the previous vertex's elevation.
fl.drawn.guessed.other: {n} vertices were off the surface and took the previous vertex's elevation.

fl.props.head: Feature line
fl.props.name: Name
fl.use.note.eg: The existing ground runs through this line at its elevations, like a breakline.
fl.use.note.design: The proposed surface inside this closed line is graded to its edge (a sloped pad). Turn on daylight to run cut and fill slopes out to the ground.
fl.use.note.design.open: Only a closed feature line can be graded into the design: close it, or use it as a breakline of the existing ground.
fl.use.note.off: The line is drawn on the plan and exported, but the surfaces do not use it.
fl.props.closed: Closed (the last vertex joins the first)
fl.props.daylight: Daylight to the ground with cut and fill slopes
fl.props.grade.of: Grade from vertex {n} to the next, in percent
fl.props.grade.note: A grade sets the elevation at the far end of its segment; the vertices after it stay where they are.

fl.arc.short: Segment {n} is too long for that radius: it needs at least {min}.

fl.arc.off: Arcs off: each click is the next vertex.
fl.arc.mid: Point on the curve set: now click where the arc ends.

fl.offset.name: {name} offset {d}
fl.surface.none: No vertex of this line is on the existing ground.
fl.surface.done: Elevations taken from the existing ground.
fl.surface.missing: Off the surface, kept as they were: vertices {list}.

codes.title: Description keys and line codes
codes.keys.lede: A key matches the field code at the start of a description (* = any characters, ? = one) and puts the point in a group, with a use and a long description. The first key that matches wins; codes no key matches stay their own group.
codes.col.label: Description
codes.lines.on: Join points into lines by line codes
codes.lines.lede: A line code is the word right after the field code: "EP B" begins a new edge-of-pavement line, "EP E" ends it, "BLDG C" closes a building back to its first corner. Points with the same code join in point-number order; EP1 and EP2 are separate lines. Breakline groups follow these lines; other groups' lines are drawn on the plan.

codes.done.one: 1 description key applied; the groups and the surface follow (Ctrl+Z undoes it).
codes.done.other: {keys} description keys applied; the groups and the surface follow (Ctrl+Z undoes it).

codes.dropped.one: 1 key with a code CivilCraft cannot read was left out (codes are letters, digits and * ? _ . - / #).
codes.dropped.other: {n} keys with codes CivilCraft cannot read were left out (codes are letters, digits and * ? _ . - / #).

se.short: Curve {n} (radius {r}) is too short for full superelevation: the transitions meet before it is reached.
se.overlap: The superelevation transitions of curves {a} and {b} overlap: lengthen the tangent between them, or check the rate table.
se.head: Superelevation
se.off.note: With superelevation on, the lanes rotate about the centerline through each curve: the outside lane flattens, then the whole road tilts toward the inside of the curve, and back after it.
se.rate.e.of: Superelevation rate of row {n}, in percent (empty = normal crown)
se.rate.note: A curve takes the rate of the first row whose radius it reaches. These rates and the 0.5 % gradient are placeholders, not a standard: set them from your own design criteria. Runoff = lane width × e ÷ the gradient; runout = normal crown ÷ e × runoff; two thirds of the runoff lies before the curve.
se.none: No curve of this alignment is sharp enough to superelevate with this table.
se.diagram.label: Superelevation diagram: the left lane's cross slope (solid) and the right lane's (dashed) along the stations; down = falls away from the center line.
co.note: Slopes fall away from the crown. Placeholders, not a standard. Superelevation is below. Build each side from parts to add curb and gutter, a planting strip and a sidewalk.
hy.no.outlet: {name} drains to no structure of the network: choose its outlet.
hy.loop: The pipes form a loop, so flows cannot be summed downstream: break the loop.
hy.full: {name} flows full (surcharged): the hydraulic grade line is above its crown.
hy.flood: The hydraulic grade line is {by} above the rim at {name}: water reaches the surface there.
dr.head: Storm drainage
dr.note: Q = C × i × A, summed down the network: each pipe carries every catchment above it at the longest time of concentration, with travel times through the pipes flowing full. i in {i}, Q in {q}, A in {a}. The intensity curve, n and the junction loss are placeholders, not a standard: set them from your own rainfall data and design criteria.
dr.hint: Catchment: click the corners of the area that drains to a structure. Enter finishes; it drains to a structure inside it, else the nearest one.
dr.none: No catchments yet. Draw the areas that drain to each structure to work out flows, pipe sizes and the hydraulic grade line.
dr.c.head: Catchment
dr.c.name: Name
dr.c.note: C is the share of the rain that runs off (0 to 1). The time of concentration is how long water takes from the farthest point of the area to its structure.
dr.c.few: A catchment needs at least three corners.
dr.c.nonet: Draw the pipe network first: a catchment drains to one of its structures.
dr.c.drawn: {name}: {a}, draining to {to}, C 0.5. Change them in Properties.
dr.ok: Every pipe flows part full and the hydraulic grade line stays below every rim.
dr.size: Size the pipes for these flows
dr.size.note: Each pipe gets the smallest standard size that carries its flow at its own slope. Inverts stay where they are: set them again from the rules if the sizes change.
rt.head: Route a storm
rt.lead: The rational method gives one peak for each pipe. This works out the whole storm: each catchment's runoff over time, carried down the pipes with their travel time and storage, and added where they meet.
rt.none: Nothing to route yet: draw a catchment that drains to a structure, and give the pipes a diameter and a fall.
rt.storm: A steady rain of {i} {u} for {d} minutes.
rt.chart: Flow over time: peak {q} {u} at {m} minutes
rt.method: Each pipe is routed with the Muskingum–Cunge method. Surcharge, backwater, storage in structures and flooding are not modelled: a pipe over its capacity is flagged, and its water is passed on as if it fitted. Use it to see timing and attenuation, not to size the pipe.
rt.nodia: {name} has no diameter, so it is not routed.
rt.flat: {name} has no fall or no length, so it is not routed.
rt.long: The storm is longer than the tool simulates: the end of the run is cut off.
rt.over: {name}: the routed peak is above its full capacity.
dr.size.same: Every pipe already has the smallest size that carries its flow.
dr.size.done: {n} pipe sizes changed (one step: Ctrl+Z undoes it).
dr.size.bad: {n} pipes need more than the largest size: make them steeper or split the flow.
dr.idf.lead: Rainfall intensity for the design storm, as i = a ÷ (tc + b) to the power c:
dr.idf.formula: Fit a, b and c to your own intensity-duration-frequency curve for the return period you design for.
pc.err.radius: A curve needs its radius: R 300.

set.order.hint: Point, northing, easting, elevation, description — or easting before northing. Used for points you copy (the rows a spreadsheet gets), point rows you paste, and the import's guess when a file has no header row.
set.renum.hint: Keep free numbers: a pasted point keeps its number when no point has it, and only clashing points are renumbered. Two points never share a number. Leave the start empty to count on from the highest number in use; with a start, new numbers count up from it, skipping any already taken.
set.labels.hint: What a point label shows when Point labels is on under Display. DXF, DWG and PDF exports show the same.
set.corner.hint: The view cube sits at the top right of the plan and the 3D view. On the plan it shows the top; click any other side, edge or corner, or drag it, to see the site in 3D from there. In 3D, click to look from a side, drag it to orbit, drag the compass ring to turn. The axis icon is a small X, Y (and Z in 3D) marker at the bottom left.
set.exag.hint: How much the 3D view stretches elevations. The list on the 3D view's bar is the same setting. Volumes, profiles and 3D exports stay at true scale.
set.latlon.hint: How the status bar shows the pointer’s latitude and longitude: degrees, minutes and seconds, or decimal degrees. It shows them only when the project has a coordinate system (GIS › Coordinates).

gexp.nothing: Nothing to export: tick at least one kind that has something in it.

gexp.grid: Coordinates were written in grid ({crs}), not the project’s ground/local numbers.

vec.layer.show.title: Show or hide this layer
vec.layer.color.title: Colour on the plan
vec.layer.more.title: More for this layer
vec.layer.removed: Removed GIS layer {layer}. Ctrl+Z brings it back.
vec.rename.title: Rename the GIS layer
vec.rename.name: Name
vec.ask.title: Choose a coordinate system
vec.ask.none: No system is suggested for this place. GIS › Coordinates sets the project’s system.
vec.ask.note: Systems whose area holds the data, in the project’s units (state plane and UTM first).
vec.import.other: Not read here: {files} (open them on their own).
vec.import.nothing: No GIS features were found in {files}.
vec.import.badcrs: {file}: its coordinate system could not be read — {why}
vec.import.project: The project is in {crs}. Layers with a system of their own are converted into it.
vec.import.project.local: The project is in {crs} (with a ground/local adjustment). Layers with a system of their own are converted into it.
vec.offer.use: Use {crs} as the project’s coordinate system
vec.offer.pick: Pick another system for the project (the layers are converted into it)…
vec.offer.will: The project’s coordinate system will be {crs}.
vec.import.nocrs: Neither the project nor the files say which coordinate system they are in, so the numbers are loaded as they are (the files must use the same coordinates as the project).
vec.unknown.legend: {file} has no .prj (it does not say its coordinate system):
vec.unknown.same: Same as the project — load its numbers as they are
vec.pick.reason: Pick the project’s coordinate system; the layers are converted into it.

vec.what.layers.one: {count} layer ({features} features) will be added as GIS layers, drawn on the plan and listed under GIS layers.
vec.what.layers.other: {count} layers ({features} features) will be added as GIS layers, drawn on the plan and listed under GIS layers.

vec.what.needs: Choose the project’s coordinate system first: data with a coordinate system is never placed by guesswork.
vec.what.convert.local: They are converted from {from} to {to} and its ground/local adjustment.
vec.what.becomes: {crs} becomes the project’s coordinate system (the same undo step).

vec.imported.one: Imported {count} GIS layer ({features} features). Click a feature with Select to see its attributes; Use for the surface is in each layer’s menu.
vec.imported.other: Imported {count} GIS layers ({features} features). Click a feature with Select to see its attributes; Use for the surface is in each layer’s menu.

vec.use.nothing: {layer} has nothing CivilCraft can use for the surface (no elevations, no number field, no polygon).
vec.use.selected: The boundary is the selected polygon (feature {n}).
vec.use.largest: The boundary is the largest polygon of the layer (select one on the plan first to use that one).
vec.use.title: Use {layer} for the surface
vec.use.note: This copies the geometry into the project (breaklines, the boundary or survey points) as one undo step; the layer stays as it is. Elevations are taken as they are, in project units.
vec.move.converted: The project and its GIS layers were converted to {crs} (the layers as a second undo step).
vec.move.title: Move the GIS layers?
vec.move.text: The GIS layers were placed for {before}. Move them to where they belong in {after}? Leave them if the project’s numbers did not change system.
vec.move.done: The GIS layers were moved to {crs}. Ctrl+Z puts them back.
vec.latlon.reason: {file} has latitude and longitude columns. Pick the project’s coordinate system so the points can be placed in easting and northing.
vec.latlon.note: The latitude and longitude were converted to {crs}; elevations were taken as they are.
vec.latlon.note.set: The latitude and longitude were converted to {crs}, now the project’s coordinate system; elevations were taken as they are.
vec.lx.unknown: {file} names a coordinate system, but {why}; the project has none. GIS › Coordinates sets one.
vec.lx.cannot: {file} says it is in {crs}, which cannot be this project’s system: {why}
vec.lx.title: Use the file’s coordinate system?
vec.lx.use: Use it as the project’s coordinate system? Nothing moves: it says what the numbers mean.
vec.lx.now: The project’s coordinate system is now {crs}.
vec.x.fmt.shp: Shapefile (.zip: one shapefile per kind, with .prj and .cpg)
vec.x.fmt.geojson: GeoJSON (one file, latitude and longitude, a "kind" property on every feature)
vec.x.coords.local: Coordinates are written in grid coordinates of {crs}. The project uses ground/local coordinates (scale {scale}), so the numbers in the file differ from the plan’s — as a GIS department expects.
vec.x.coords.local.rot: Coordinates are written in grid coordinates of {crs}. The project uses ground/local coordinates (scale {scale}, rotation {rotation}°), so the numbers in the file differ from the plan’s — as a GIS department expects.
vec.x.coords: Coordinates are written in {crs}, the project’s system; shapefiles get a .prj and GeoPackages the system’s EPSG code.
vec.x.coords.none: The project has no coordinate system: shapefiles and GeoPackages carry the project’s own numbers and name no system (tell the receiver which system they are in, or set one in GIS › Coordinates first). GeoJSON needs a system.
vec.x.units.m: Lengths, stations and elevations are in metres (the project’s units); pipe and structure diameters in millimetres (DIA_UNIT); SLOPE in percent. GeoJSON heights are in metres, as RFC 7946 asks. Shapefile field names are cut to 10 characters.
vec.x.units.ft: Lengths, stations and elevations are in US survey feet (the project’s units); pipe and structure diameters in inches (DIA_UNIT); SLOPE in percent. GeoJSON heights are in metres, as RFC 7946 asks. Shapefile field names are cut to 10 characters.
vec.x.title: Export as-built data for GIS
crs.d.search.ph: Code or name: 2277, Texas Central, UTM 14N…
crs.d.grid.note: The project’s coordinates are the system’s own grid coordinates (state plane, UTM…). Most projects are drawn this way.
crs.d.ground.note: Ground coordinates: distances on the plan are true distances on the ground. Grid = base + combined factor × (ground − base).
crs.d.base.note: The base point is where ground and grid coordinates are the same. Most jurisdictions scale about 0,0, so ground coordinates stay recognizably close to grid ones; some use the project’s control point instead — use what the survey says.
crs.d.factor.head: Compute the factor at a point
crs.d.pick.point: Pick a point on the plan
crs.d.local.note: An assumed site grid (5000, 5000 …) tied to the system by two control points: pick each survey point (type its number or click it on the plan), then type its grid coordinates — or its latitude and longitude.
crs.d.pick.head: Pick a system
crs.d.change.head: Change the system
crs.d.none: {none} — coordinates are just numbers. Pick the system the survey is in to see latitude and longitude, use GIS files and map layers.
crs.d.match.near: {count} systems match “{q}”, those whose area holds the place first.
crs.d.nomatch: No system matches “{q}”. Try the EPSG code, or fewer words.

crs.d.fit.one: Systems these coordinates fit: {n} system in {unit} put the project’s middle (E {e}, N {n2}) inside their area of use.
crs.d.fit.other: Systems these coordinates fit: {n} systems in {unit} put the project’s middle (E {e}, N {n2}) inside their area of use.

crs.d.fit.first: The first {n} are shown; search to narrow them.
crs.d.fit.none: No system in {unit} puts the project’s middle (E {e}, N {n}) inside its area of use: the coordinates may be local (an assumed grid), or in another unit. Search by name, or pick near a place.
crs.d.near.bad: Type a latitude and longitude, for example 30.27, -97.74 or 30°16′N 97°44′W.
crs.d.near.list: Projected systems whose area holds {place}, national and state grids first:
crs.d.near.none: No projected system in the list covers that place.
crs.d.list.start: Search by EPSG code or name, or type where the site is and choose Suggest.
crs.d.chosen.keep: Keep the system above, or pick another.
crs.d.mid: Read in this system, the project’s middle is at {at}.
crs.d.mid.in: Read in this system, the project’s middle is at {at}, inside its area of use.
crs.d.mid.out: Read in this system, the project’s middle is at {at} — outside the system’s area of use. If the coordinates are local, use Local below.
crs.d.mid.cannot: The project’s coordinates are outside what this system can convert.
crs.d.factor.en: Type the point’s E and N, or pick it on the plan.
crs.d.factor.z: The elevation is not a number.
crs.d.factor.out: That point is outside what the system can convert.
crs.d.k.v: {k} ({ppm}) — how much the map projection stretches distances here
crs.d.ef.v: {f} ({ppm}) — how much shorter distances are at sea level than at {z} {unit}
crs.d.conv.v: {deg}° — the angle from grid north to true north (geodetic azimuth = grid azimuth + this)
crs.d.geoid: The elevation is taken as height above the ellipsoid: without a geoid model the elevation factor can be off by about 5 ppm for every 30 m (100 ft) of geoid height. Use the factor the survey states when it gives one.
crs.d.cp.err.ll: Control point {n}: type its latitude and longitude, for example 30.27, -97.74.
crs.d.cp.err.out: Control point {n}: that place is outside what the system can convert.
crs.d.cp.err.num: Control point {n}: the grid E and N must be numbers.
crs.d.local.need: Two control points, each with its grid coordinates (or latitude and longitude), set the local grid.
crs.d.l.rot.v: {deg}° counterclockwise from the local grid to the system’s
crs.d.l.fit.v: Two points always fit exactly — check a third.
crs.d.check: Check point: the fit puts it {d} {unit} from its grid coordinates (ΔE {dx}, ΔN {dy}).
crs.d.check.ppm: Check point: the fit puts it {d} {unit} from its grid coordinates (ΔE {dx}, ΔN {dy}, {ppm} ppm of the distance from control point 1).
crs.d.check.need: Give the check point both a survey point and its grid coordinates.
crs.d.err.csf: Type the combined scale factor (about 0.9999 or 1.0001), or compute it at a point.
crs.d.err.base: The base point E and N must be numbers (0, 0 is common).
crs.d.err.local: Local coordinates need two control points with their grid coordinates.
crs.d.err.scale: The two control points give a scale of {s}: check the points and their units.
crs.d.click.factor: Click the point to compute the scale factor at. Esc goes back.
crs.d.click.cp: Click the survey point for control point {n}. Esc goes back.
crs.d.click.miss: Click on a survey point (or type its number).
crs.d.prj.big: {file} is too large to be a .prj file.
crs.d.apply.none: Pick a system first, or Cancel.

crs.d.converted: Converted {count} coordinates into {crs}. Ctrl+Z undoes it.
crs.d.set: The project is in {crs}. Nothing moved.

st.none: No structure types yet. A type is a structure you build from its shape and sizes, use for any structure of the network and save as a library item.

st.item.saved: Saved {name}: upload it to the library to share the structure.
st.item.desc: Pipe network structure made in CivilCraft's structure builder: {words}.

st.lib.opened: Structure type {name} added from the library item.
st.max: A network holds at most {n} structure types.

st.saved: Structure type {name} saved: structures of this type follow it.

geo.tower.util: Leg use of the capacity you gave
geo.cover.covered: Area at or above the receiver sensitivity
geo.cover.note: A planning sketch: free-space loss plus the worst ridge on each straight path (knife edge, ITU-R P.526). It leaves out several ridges in a row, rain, trees you did not enter and antenna patterns, so it is a little optimistic. Green is 20 dB or more above the sensitivity, yellow 10 to 20, orange up to 10.
geo.prob.tel-cover-fine: {item}: the cells are too small for this radius ({cells} cells). Use a larger cell size.
geo.prob.tel-cover-noground: {item}: the transmitter is not over known ground, so nothing was calculated.
geo.prob.tel-leg-over: {item}: the tower leg carries {util} % of the capacity you gave (with your load factor). This is statics only: your tower code decides.
geo.prob.tel-leg-buckling: {item}: the leg load is {util} % of its Euler buckling load. Brace it closer or use a bigger section.
geo.lead.covers: Where a transmitter can be heard over the existing ground: received power cell by cell, shaded on the plan.
river.join.head: Junction
river.join.note: If this river flows into another, the two are solved together: the flows add, and this river ends at the water surface of the one it joins. The river it joins carries the sum of the rivers that flow into it, so to join a main river and a creek, draw a short river below the junction and let both flow into it.
river.join.undo: Set what the river flows into
river.join.method: Equal water surface method: the joining rivers end at the water level of the main river's first section. It leaves out the angle between them and the momentum of the flows, so it suits slow, deep water and is rough where the flow is fast. Same labelled default as the rest: needs an engineer's review.
river.join.issue.profilecount: The rivers that join must have the same number of flow profiles (profile 1 of each is the same event). Fix {id}.
river.join.issue.oneoutlet: The joined rivers must end in exactly one outlet.
river.join.issue.joincycle: The rivers flow into each other in a loop.
river.join.issue.joinmissing: {id} flows into a river that does not exist.
sx.su957.defaults: Defaults in these results, kept until an engineer reviews them: contraction 0.1 and expansion 0.3; the channel as one piece with a composite roughness; the mixed regime chosen by specific force without placing the jump; the flood extent includes low ground inside the corridor that the water cannot reach unless you drew a levee. Change any of them in the river's Properties.
rail.std.note: Choose the standard these limits are for. No number from any standard is built in: you (or the railway's engineer) type each value, and the clause it comes from beside it.
rail.std.placeholder: Every number in this window, in the turnouts and in the structure gauge is still a placeholder, whatever standard is named. A railway engineer checks each value against the standard's own text before anything is built.
pl.don.readuntested: Untested: the reader was built from a list of field names, not from a real study file. Check every support against your own file.
geo.import.untested: Untested on real files: the RW5, GSI, JobXML and CSV readers were written from each format's public description and tried only on files we made. Check the points and observations against your instrument's own report.

scanin.cmd.title: Bring in a sheet from a scanner, a photo or a PDF (a plat, survey, grading plan or sketch), place it to scale or on known coordinates and convert it into a drawing
scanin.title: Start from a scan: {file}
scanin.lede: The sheet goes under the plan as a picture, to scale or on coordinates you know, and its lines can be traced onto a layer you can turn into a boundary or breaklines. It is read on this computer; nothing is uploaded.
scanin.straight.weak: (the sheet may be {deg}° off square; the lines were too few to be sure)
scanin.straight.photo: (the sheet was found in the photo and is shown straight on)
scanin.straight.nosheet: (no sheet edge was found in the photo; it is used as it is)
scanin.view.label: The sheet. Wheel to zoom, drag to move, click to mark a point.
scanin.place.head: Where it goes
scanin.help.two: Click both ends of something whose length you know (a bearing and distance, a dimension, the scale bar), then type that length.
scanin.help.stated: Use the scale printed on the sheet. This is only right when the scan was made at true size at the dpi given: check a known length afterwards.
scanin.help.pts: Click a point on the sheet (a property corner, a monument, a grid crossing), then type its easting and northing or the number of a survey point already in the project. Two points place, turn and scale the sheet; a third checks the others.
scanin.pts.stretch: Let the sheet stretch differently across and down (paper that shrank or a scanner that pulled; needs three points)
scanin.need.two: Click two points on the sheet.
scanin.need.dist: Type the true distance between the two points ({unit}).
scanin.need.stated: Give the dpi the sheet was scanned at and its printed scale.
scanin.need.pts2: Mark at least two points and give each its coordinates or a survey point.
scanin.need.pts3: Mark at least three points (not in one line) to let the sheet stretch.
scanin.need.spread: The points are in one place or in one line: spread them across the sheet.
scanin.then.head: Then
scanin.trace: Convert it into a drawing (its lines and arcs on a layer of their own)
scanin.trace.note: Lettering and hatching stay on the picture. The drawing is a starting point, not a survey: check it against the sheet. You can also convert later from the Scans list.
scanin.trace.big: The sheet is too big to trace in one go; it was placed without a trace.
scanin.what.head: What you get
scanin.what.rms: The points agree to {rms} {unit} (root mean square).
scanin.what.unchecked: With only the points needed, nothing checks them: add one more to see how well they agree.
scanin.what.scale: That is 1 inch = {per} {unit} on the sheet as scanned.
scanin.err.kind: {file} is not a PDF, TIFF, PNG or JPEG.
scanin.err.pdf: {file} is a PDF, and PDF pages cannot be read here.
scanin.done.traced: Converted it into a drawing: {n} lines on the layer "{layer}". Use for the surface makes a boundary or breaklines of them. Keep the scan as a reference or remove it in the Scans list.
scanin.how.points-stretch: on known coordinates, stretched to fit
scanin.why.not_scan: it is not a PNG, JPEG or TIFF
scanin.why.size: the picture has no usable size
scanin.why.pixels: it has more than 100 million pixels
scanin.why.damaged: the file is damaged or cut off
scanin.why.page: that page is not in the file
scanin.why.tiled: the TIFF is stored in tiles (save it again with strips)
scanin.why.planar: the TIFF keeps its colours in separate planes
scanin.why.bits: the TIFF uses a sample size that is not read
scanin.why.samples: the TIFF has a number of samples a pixel that is not read
scanin.why.photometric: the TIFF uses a colour model that is not read
scanin.why.compression: the TIFF compression is not read (uncompressed, PackBits, LZW and Group 4 are)
scanin.why.predictor: the TIFF uses a predictor that is not read
scanin.why.interlaced: the PNG is interlaced (save it again without interlacing)
scanin.why.format: the picture format is not read
scanin.why.progressive: the progressive JPEG could not be decoded
scanin.why.jpeg: the JPEG uses something that is not read
scanin.why.trace_big: it is too big to trace
scanin.drop.ask: {file} has no world file. Place it as a scanned sheet?
scanin.what.which: One more point tells which one is off, if one is.
cad.sv.head: Survey levels and check
cad.sv.lede: Levels written as text next to a point, or in a block attribute, are not lines, so they are not read as linework. Take them as survey points, and check the drawing before you build ground from it.
cad.sv.take: Take {n} levels as survey points ({text} from text, {attr} from block attributes)
cad.sv.none: No levels written as text or block attributes were found.
cad.sv.tag: Block attribute that holds the level
cad.sv.tag.auto: Find it by name (ELEV, Z, LEVEL …)
cad.sv.what: {n} survey points with levels from text and attributes.
cad.sv.check.head: Check before use
cad.sv.check.clean: Nothing found: the units, distance from the origin, contours, levels and points look right.
cad.sv.issues: The check found {n} things to look at; they are listed in Problems.
survey.p.units.none: The drawing does not say what its units are; it is read as {unit}. Check a known distance.
survey.p.units.scaled: The drawing's units are converted to {unit} (x {scale}).
survey.p.units.big: The data spans about {km} km. The drawing may be in millimetres or another unit than the one it says.
survey.p.units.small: The data spans {m} m. The drawing may be in metres but read as millimetres, or drawn tiny.
survey.p.crs.none: No coordinate system is known for this drawing.
survey.p.origin.far: The data lies about {km} km from the origin (centre near {x}, {y}). Far from zero, 3D views lose precision and shake.
survey.p.contours.flat: Contour layer {layer}: {flat} of {all} lines have no height (flat at 0). A ground built from them would be flat.
survey.p.z.zero: {n} levels are exactly 0 while the typical level is {median}. They look like missing heights.
survey.p.z.outlier: {n} levels are far from the rest (typical {median}; expected between {low} and {high}).
survey.p.dup.same: {n} points sit on top of another point at the same level.
survey.p.dup.level: {n} points sit on top of another point with a different level.
scanin.src.title: Scan
scanin.src.lede: Where does the sheet come from? Whatever it is, it becomes a scan: placed under the plan and converted into a drawing, and kept or removed when you are done with it.
scanin.src.noscanner: Scanning straight from a scanner needs CadCraft Studio on a computer. Here, scan to a folder or to email on the copier and choose the file, or take a photo.
scanin.sc.looking: Looking for scanners on this network…
scanin.sc.found: Found {n}. Put the sheet on the scanner and press Scan.
scanin.sc.none: No scanner answered on this network. Network scanners and copiers that support AirScan or Mopria show here; for a USB scanner, scan to a file and choose the file.
scanin.sc.name: Scan {when}
scanin.sc.err.busy: {name} is busy. Try again when it is free.
scanin.sc.err.refused: {name} refused the scan. Check that a sheet is on the glass or in the feeder.
scanin.sc.err.nopage: {name} sent no page. Check that a sheet is on the glass or in the feeder.
scanin.sc.err.network: {name} could not be reached. Look again, or check that it is on and on this network.
scanin.list.head: Scans
scanin.list.need: {n} waiting for you to keep or remove
scanin.list.note: A scan stays here until you decide: keep it as a reference under the plan, or remove it once its drawing is made. The drawing is a layer of its own and stays either way.
scanin.list.new: Placed. Not converted into a drawing yet.
scanin.list.drawn: Converted into a drawing ({n} lines). Keep the scan as a reference, or remove it?
scanin.list.kept: Kept as a reference under the plan.
scanin.list.kept.drawn: Converted ({n} lines) and kept as a reference under the plan.
scanin.list.remove.scan: Remove the scan, keep the drawing
scanin.list.remove.both: Remove the scan and its drawing
scanin.undo.remove.both: Remove the scan {name} and its drawing
scanin.converted: Converted {name} into a drawing: {n} lines on the layer "{layer}".
scanin.converted.none: Nothing on {name} could be converted into lines.
scanin.kept: Kept {name} as a reference under the plan.
scanin.removed: Removed the scan {name}; its drawing stays.
scanin.removed.both: Removed the scan {name} and its drawing.
